note.question: How should an organization decide when a team stops producing to coordinate, and how should meeting rules change with worker heterogeneity and team size?
note.overview: Workers repeatedly state whether they prefer production or coordination under an organizational scheduling rule. The paper studies dominant-strategy Markov-perfect equilibria and compares decentralized rule-induced outcomes with a first-best dynamic policy.

models.name: Dynamic production-versus-coordination game under worker-driven and time-based meeting rules
models.summary: Workers repeatedly state whether they prefer production or coordination under an organizational scheduling rule. The paper studies dominant-strategy Markov-perfect equilibria and compares decentralized rule-induced outcomes with a first-best dynamic policy.

An organizational designer that selects the coordination scheduling rule

Worker-driven rules observe only the vector of stated preferences
The first-best benchmark observes the full vector of accumulated issues
Issue arrivals follow a stationary distribution known to the workers and designer
decisions: Each worker states a preference for coordination or production

models.method: The authors formulate worker-specific dynamic programs, derive the first-best threshold policy, solve the two-worker model analytically, establish worst-case efficiency bounds, and use analytical asymptotics plus numerical comparisons to study larger teams, voting rules, safeguards, and fixed meeting intervals.

components.label: Information structure
components.explanation: A worker's current coordination needs determine that worker's production value and stated preference. Worker-driven rules observe only the vector of stated preferences, while time-based rules also observe elapsed time since the last coordination period. The first-best benchmark observes the full vector of accumulated issues. Issue arrivals follow a stationary distribution known to the workers and designer.
